title: Prostate Cancer DEG Analysis (GSE6919)
text:
In this analysis, I used bulk RNA sequencing (microarray data) from the public GEO dataset GSE6919 to investigate differences in gene expression between cancerous and healthy prostate tissues.
The aim was to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) that could point to disrupted biological processes in prostate cancer, especially with a view toward metabolic shifts or biomarker discovery.

The analysis was performed in R using the following packages:

GEOquery — to load expression and metadata

limma — for linear modeling of microarray data

tidyverse — for data wrangling and exploration

clusterProfiler, org.Hs.eg.db — for GO enrichment analysis

Downloaded GSE6919 and extracted the expression matrix

Cleaned and labeled metadata (e.g. tumor vs. normal)

Fit a linear model using limma and contrasted tumor vs. normal

Extracted top upregulated and downregulated genes

What’s Holding AI Back in Biology?

Current issues with Ai in biosciences:


Reproducibility issues — hard to trust models without transparent workflows.
Learning curve and training — lack of experience with AI was a significant pain point for many users.

title: Day 8: Rosalind Problems – Independent Alleles, Protein Motif & Shared Motif
text:
Compute the probability that at least (N) of the (2^k) offspring have genotype Aa Bb, given every parent is Aa Bb.
My solution
import math

def independent_assortment(k: int, N: int) -> float:
    """
    P(X ≥ N) where X ~ Binomial(n = 2**k, p = 1/4).
    Each of the 2**k offspring has p = 1/4 chance of Aa Bb.
    """
    n = 2**k
    p = 1/4
    prob = 0.0
    # sum the right‐hand tail of the binomial distribution
    for i in range(N, n+1):
        prob += math.comb(n, i) * p**i * (1-p)**(n-i)
    return prob

if __name__ == "__main__":
    k, N = 5, 8
    print(f"{independent_assortment(k, N):.6f}")


Binomial “tail” sums The probability of getting at least (N) successes out of (n) trials with success rate (p) is \[
    P(X \ge N)
    \;=\;
    \sum_{i=N}^{n} \binom{n}{i}\,p^i\,(1-p)^{\,n-i}\,.
  \] Implemented in Python by summing from i = N to n of math.comb(n, i) * p**i * (1-p)**(n-i).

Exact binomial coefficients
Python 3.8+’s math.comb(n, i) computes () directly and exactly.
Off‑by‑one vigilance
Translating between 0‑based loops (Python) and 1‑based math notation (Rosalind) requires adding or subtracting 1 at the right spots.

title: Day 8: Rosalind Problems – Independent Alleles, Protein Motif & Shared Motif
text:
Problem 2: Finding a Protein Motif
Locate every occurrence (including overlaps) of the N‑glycosylation motif N{P}[ST]{P} in a set of UniProt sequences.
My solution
from Bio import SeqIO

def get_substrings(s):
    """
    Generate all possible substrings of the input string s,
    returning them from longest to shortest.

    Parameters:
        s (str): The string from which to generate substrings.

    Returns:
        List[str]: A list of every substring of s, ordered by decreasing length.
    """
    substrs = []             # Will hold all substrings
    n = len(s)               # Total length of the string

    # For each possible substring length L from n down to 1
    for L in range(n, 0, -1):
        # Slide a window of length L along the string
        # i goes from 0 up to n - L
        for i in range(n - L + 1):
            # Extract the substring of length L starting at i
            substrs.append(s[i:i + L])
    return substrs          # Return all substrings, longest first

def longest_common_substring_bruteforce(records):
    """
    Find the longest substring common to all sequences in the provided SeqRecord list,
    using a brute‑force approach.

    """
    # Convert each SeqRecord to a plain Python string
    seqs = [str(rec.seq) for rec in records]

    # Sort by length so the shortest sequence is first
    # We only need to generate substrings from the shortest one
    seqs.sort(key=len)
    shortest = seqs[0]       # The sequence to pull substrings from
    others = seqs[1:]        # The rest of the sequences

    # Generate substrings from longest to shortest
    for sub in get_substrings(shortest):
        # Check if this substring appears in every other sequence
        if all(sub in seq for seq in others):
            return sub       # As soon as one matches all, it's the LCS

    return ""  # If no common substring is found (edge case), return empty




if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Parse the FASTA file (make sure the filename matches exactly)
    records = list(SeqIO.parse("rosalind_lcsm (2).fasta", "fasta"))

    # Compute the longest common substring
    result = longest_common_substring_bruteforce(records)

    # Output the result
    print("Brute‑force LCS:", result)

What I learned:

Zero‑width look‑ahead ((?=…)) lets the engine test every offset without skipping—so overlapping motifs (e.g. positions 276 and 278) are both found.
Translating PROSITE shorthand (N{P}[ST]{P}) to regex (N[^P][ST][^P]).
Robust HTTP fetch with raise_for_status() to catch bad accessions early.

# Compile the PROSITE motif using a look‑ahead so we catch overlaps
# (?=(…)) is zero‑width, so the regex engine checks at every position without skipping
motif = re.compile(r"(?=(N[^P][ST][^P]))")

def fetch_sequence(accession: str) -> str:
    """
    Given a UniProt accession (optionally with "_NAME" suffix),
    fetch its protein FASTA from UniProt and return the concatenated sequence.
    """
    # Strip off anything after the first underscore
    acc = accession.split("_", 1)[0]
    url = f"https://www.uniprot.org/uniprot/{acc}.fasta"
    resp = requests.get(url)
    resp.raise_for_status()
    lines = resp.text.splitlines()
    # Skip the header (first line) and join the rest into one sequence string
    return "".join(lines[1:])

def find_motif_positions(seq: str) -> list[str]:
    """
    Scan `seq` for the N‑glycosylation motif N{P}[ST]{P},
    returning all 1‑based start positions (including overlaps).
    """
    # m.start() is 0‑based, so add 1 for Rosalind’s 1‑based indexing
    return [str(m.start() + 1) for m in motif.finditer(seq)]

def main():
    # Read your list of raw UniProt IDs (one per line) from ids_mprt.txt
    with open("ids_mprt.txt") as f:
        raw_ids = [line.strip() for line in f if line.strip()]

    for raw in raw_ids:
        seq = fetch_sequence(raw)
        positions = find_motif_positions(seq)
        if positions:
            # Print the original raw ID, then the space‑separated positions
            print(raw)
            print(" ".join(positions))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

What I learned:

Sorting by length ensures we find the longest common substring early and exit.

title: Day 6: Rosalind Problems – Mortal Fibonacci & Consensus DNA
text:
Problem 1: Mortal Fibonacci Rabbits
Simulated rabbit population growth over 89 months with a fixed lifespan of 18 months.
my solution
n = 89  # Total months
m = 18  # Lifespan in months

def mortal_fibonacci(n, m):
    ages = [1] + [0] * (m - 1) # max array length = m

    for month in range(1, n):
        new_borns = sum(ages[1:])  # rabbits of age ≥1 can reproduce
        # Age rabbits: shift right, oldest dies
        ages = [new_borns] + ages[:-1]

    return sum(ages)
print(mortal_fibonacci(n, m))

What I learned:

ages[1:] ensures only mature rabbits reproduce.
arrays have an interesting usecase due to its max capacity.

AWS Account ID

Every AWS account has a unique 12-digit ID.

AWS Tools for PowerShell

Built on .NET command language.

Browser-based shell built into the AWS Console.

Declarative templates (JSON or YAML).

Imperative code (Python, TypeScript, Java, etc.) that compiles to CloudFormation.

Shared Responsibility Model

AWS is responsible for Security of the Cloud:

Global infrastructure, physical security, compute/storage/networking layers.


Customer is responsible for Security in the Cloud:

Availability Zones (AZs)

AZ = one or more data centers in a secured building with hundreds of thousands of servers.

A region typically contains 3 AZs.

AZs are physically isolated (different buildings, power, cooling) but close enough for low-latency communication.

Best practice: run workloads across ≥3 AZs for high uptime.

Subnets are tied to an AZ → when you create a VM (EC2 instance), it is associated with a subnet within that AZ.




Fault Tolerance & Fault Domains

Fault tolerance = system’s ability to continue operating despite component failures.

Fault domain: A logical boundary that limits the impact of failures.

Example: contamination zone analogy.

In Azure: you define fault domains manually.

In AWS: handled automatically.


AWS mapping:

Region = fault level.

AZ = fault domain.





AWS Global Network

AWS global backbone infrastructure = connects all regions worldwide.

Supports low-latency communication and high availability.


Edge Locations

Used for CloudFront CDN caching and AWS Global Accelerator.

Improves latency by routing user requests to the nearest PoP.



Points of Presence (PoPs)

Intermediate network locations between AWS data centers and users.

Two types:

Edge Locations: cache popular content.

Regional Edge Caches: hold larger and less frequently accessed content.




Local Zones

Data centers placed close to major population centers.

Provide low ms latency for workloads (gaming, video, AR/VR).

Must request access via AWS Support.



Wavelength Zones

Provide edge computing for 5G networks.

Enables ultra-low latency for mobile applications.

AWS partnerships: Vodafone, Verizon, SK Telecom.

Architecture: AWS Cloud ↔︎ 5G Tower ↔︎ End User Device.





Data Residency & Sovereignty

Data residency = physical/geographic location where resources or data are stored.

Compliance boundaries = regulatory restrictions on where data can reside.

Data sovereignty = legal jurisdiction or authority that governs data.

Example: EU GDPR vs US HIPAA requirements.




AWS Outposts

Physical rack of AWS servers installed on-premises at customer sites.

Provides AWS services locally while remaining managed by AWS.

Supports workloads needing low latency or data residency compliance.

AWS Config can enforce compliance rules (e.g., explicit IAM policies to restrict region access).




AWS for Government

Public Sector

Includes: military, law enforcement, healthcare, public education, transportation.

Must meet strict regulatory compliance standards.



GovCloud (US)

Isolated AWS regions designed for sensitive government workloads.

Supports FedRAMP compliance.

Accessible only to vetted US government customers and contractors.



AWS in China

Operates as isolated service regions.

Cannot connect directly to the global AWS network.

Complies with local regulatory requirements.





Key Takeaways

Availability Zones = fault domains, designed for high availability and low latency.

Global Network includes Edge Locations, Regional Edge Caches, Local Zones, and Wavelength Zones.

Data residency and sovereignty are crucial for compliance.

Outposts and GovCloud/China regions provide specialised solutions for regulated workloads.

Evolution of Computing

Dedicated Servers

A physical server allocated to a single client (single-node cluster).

Limitations:

No ability to resize or scale virtually.

Expensive (often overpaying for unused capacity).

Cannot easily replace or repurpose.

Typically limited to one application.


Advantage: Potentially very secure — if you manage security yourself.




Virtual Machines (VMs)

Use a hypervisor to run multiple VMs on a shared physical server.

Pros:

Fraction of the cost of dedicated servers.

Easier to scale compared to bare metal.

Multiple apps can run across VMs.


Cons:

Still overpaying if underutilised.

Bound by the guest operating system.





Containers

Containers run on top of VMs, managed by a Docker daemon (or similar).

Pros:

Cost-effective, maximise server capacity.

Shared OS between multiple containers → efficient.

Multiple apps per container image.


Cons:

Can be harder to maintain at scale without orchestration (e.g., Kubernetes).





Functions (Serverless)

Managed VMs running managed containers (AWS Lambda).

Serverless computing: upload code, choose memory, AWS handles the rest.

Pros:

Minimal setup required.

Cost-effective (pay only for execution time).


Cons:

Cold starts: first run can be slow as the VM/container initializes.

Software as a Service (SaaS)

A complete product run and managed by the provider.

Example: Gmail, Office 365.



Platform as a Service (PaaS)

For developers → focus on app deployment and management.

Example: Heroku, Google App Engine, Azure App Service.



Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)

Basic building blocks of cloud: networking, compute, storage.

Example: AWS, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud.





Key Takeaways

Cloud computing evolved from dedicated → VMs → containers → serverless functions, each step improving efficiency and scalability.

Service models progress from IaaS → PaaS → SaaS, with decreasing customer management responsibility.

title: Day 26 Rosaland problem — Shortest Common Supersequence
text:
Given two DNA strings s and t, return a shortest common supersequence (SCS) — the shortest string that contains both s and t as subsequences.
Key relationship with LCS:
 = (s) + (t) - 
We first compute the LCS length table (dp) and then backtrack to construct one SCS: - Match (diagonal): append the shared base once and move ↖ - Mismatch (choose path): - If dp[i-1][j] >= dp[i][j-1]: move ↑ and append s[i-1] - Else: move ← and append t[j-1] - After the main walk, append any remaining tail of s or t - Reverse the accumulated characters at the end

Method (Today’s Core Steps)

Parse gzipped FASTA with SeqIO.parse.
For each transcript, generate 6 reading frames:

Forward: F0, F1, F2

Reverse complement: R0, R1, R2


Trim frame slices so length is a multiple of 3 before translating (removes “partial codon” warnings).
Translate without stopping (to_stop=False).
Extract ORFs that start at M and end at *, with length ≥ 30 aa.
Write CSV rows: transcript_id, frame, orf_length_aa, protein_seq, gene_symbol, biotype.

text:
Reference Code (collapsed)
# ORF scan + CSV write 
import os, gzip, csv
from Bio import SeqIO
from Bio.Seq import Seq

FASTA_GZ = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "data", "gencode.v44.transcripts.fa.gz")
OUT_CSV  = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "orfs_output.csv")

MIN_LEN_AA          = 30
ONLY_PROTEIN_CODING = False   # set True to restrict to coding transcripts
MAX_TRANSCRIPTS     = 200     # bump as desired

def parse_gencode_header(desc: str):
    p = desc.split("|")
    return {
        "transcript_id": p[0] if len(p)>0 else "",
        "gene_id":       p[1] if len(p)>1 else "",
        "tx_name":       p[4] if len(p)>4 else "",
        "gene_symbol":   p[5] if len(p)>5 else "",
        "length_nt":     p[6] if len(p)>6 else "",
        "biotype":       p[7] if len(p)>7 else "",
    }

def translate_frame(nuc: Seq, frame: int) -> Seq:
    sub = nuc[frame:]
    sub = sub[:len(sub) - (len(sub) % 3)] if len(sub) >= 3 else Seq("")
    return sub.translate(to_stop=False)

def six_frame_proteins(dna: Seq):
    rc = dna.reverse_complement()
    prots = []
    for frame in range(3):
        prots += [translate_frame(dna, frame), translate_frame(rc, frame)]
    return prots  # F0,F1,F2,R0,R1,R2

def find_orfs_in_protein(prot: str, min_len_aa: int = 30):
    orfs, cur = [], None
    for aa in prot:
        if aa == "M":
            cur = "M"
        elif aa == "*":
            if cur and len(cur) >= min_len_aa:
                orfs.append(cur)
            cur = None
        elif cur:
            cur += aa
    return orfs

def scan_one_transcript(record, min_len_aa=30):
    names = ["F0","F1","F2","R0","R1","R2"]
    out = []
    for i, prot in enumerate(six_frame_proteins(record.seq)):
        for orf in find_orfs_in_protein(str(prot), min_len_aa=min_len_aa):
            out.append((record.id, names[i], len(orf), orf))
    return out

# Write CSV

SQL Basics

The Two Required Clauses: SELECT and FROM
Every SQL query begins with:
SELECT column1, column2
FROM table_name;
SELECT specifies which columns you want to see.
FROM defines which table to pull from.
Note: You can only run one SELECT statement at a time.


Limiting results

LIMIT 10;
Note: used to prevent long wait times when querying large datasets


Filtering with WHERE
SELECT *

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from pathlib import Path
from datetime import datetime
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

"""----- 1 Load one file -----"""
csv_path = Path("clinvar_clustered_pairs_1000bp.csv")
DTYPES = {
    "chrom": "string", "pos1": "Int64", "pos2": "Int64",
    "distance_bp": "Int64", "rs1": "string", "rs2": "string",
    "genes1": "string", "genes2": "string", "shared_genes": "string",
}
df = pd.read_csv(csv_path, dtype=DTYPES, low_memory=False)

# If distance not present or has NAs, recompute from pos1/pos2
if "distance_bp" not in df or df["distance_bp"].isna().any():
    df["distance_bp"] = (df[["pos1","pos2"]].max(axis=1) - df[["pos1","pos2"]].min(axis=1)).astype("Int64")

""" ----- 2 Simple stats -----"""
dist = df["distance_bp"].dropna().astype(int)
same_gene_frac = (df["shared_genes"].fillna("") != "").mean()

summary = {
    "run_time": datetime.now().isoformat(timespec="seconds"),
    "file": csv_path.name,
    "n_pairs": int(len(df)),
    "same_gene_fraction": round(float(same_gene_frac), 4),
    "dist_min": int(dist.min()) if len(dist) else None,
    "dist_median": float(np.median(dist)) if len(dist) else None,
    "dist_mean": round(float(dist.mean()), 2) if len(dist) else None,
    "dist_p95": float(np.percentile(dist, 95)) if len(dist) else None,
}
# tightness thresholds
for thr in (10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1000):
    summary[f"frac_≤{thr}bp"] = round(float((dist <= thr).mean()), 4) if len(dist) else None

print(summary)

""" ----- 3 Log the stats to a persistent CSV -----"""
log_path = Path("cluster_metrics_log.csv")
log_df = pd.DataFrame([summary])
if log_path.exists():
    log_df.to_csv(log_path, mode="a", header=False, index=False)
else:
    log_df.to_csv(log_path, index=False)
print(f"Appended metrics to {log_path}")

""" ----- 4 Tiny extra artifacts -----"""
# Top chromosomes
top_chroms = df["chrom"].value_counts().head(10)
top_chroms.to_csv("top_chroms.csv")

# Top genes by appearance (genes1 + genes2)
def split_genes(series):
    genes = []
    for s in series.fillna(""):
        genes.extend([g for g in str(s).split(";") if g])
    return genes

top_genes = (
    pd.Series(split_genes(df["genes1"]) + split_genes(df["genes2"]))
      .value_counts()
      .head(20)
)

# Linear (zoomed to ≤500 bp so you see the peak)
plt.hist(dist[dist <= 500], bins=50)
plt.xlabel("Clustered pair distance (bp) — zoom ≤ 500")
plt.ylabel("Count")
plt.title("Cluster tightness (zoom)")
plt.show()

top_genes.to_csv("top_genes.csv")
print("Wrote top_chroms.csv and top_genes.csv")

Python (pandas), Enrichr, g:Profiler The data set was used from here.
The CSV contains the transcriptomic data of 2 groups

Purkinje cell protein 4 (PCP4) is a gene which plays a role in modulating of Ca²⁺/calmodulin signaling in immune cells. It downregulates proinflamatory cytokines IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1β. Cells over expressing PCP4 have disrupted calcium homeostasis, creating a calcium-rich cytosolic environment creating a vulnerability to calcium-dependent membrane and mitochondrial damage such as ACP’s (anticancer peptides).
Although PCP4 upregulation would enhance ACP’s cytotoxicity its a mutation which is typically found within early-stage tumor development and downregulated once metastasis begins. Counteracting the specificity provided by Mastoparan Bs, which normally targets by products of of altered cellular metabolism (accumulation of lactate in the cellular membrane). text:
Given: A permutation π of length 𝑛 Return: A longest increasing subsequence of π, followed by a longest decreasing subsequence of π. My solution

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Longest Increasing/Decreasing Subsequence via Dynamic Programming

We scan forward through each position `i` in the input permutation `pi`.
At each `i`, we look back at all earlier positions `j < i` and see whether we can
extend the best subsequence ending at `j` by adding `pi[i]`.

- We maintain `L_inc[i]`: length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at `i`.
- We maintain `P_inc[i]`: pointer to the previous index in that subsequence.

Specifically, for each `i`:
    for each `j < i`:
        if `pi[j] < pi[i]` and `L_inc[j] + 1 > L_inc[i]`:
            update `L_inc[i] = L_inc[j] + 1`
            record `P_inc[i] = j`

This reuses previously computed `L_inc[j]` values (never recomputing them)—
the hallmark of dynamic programming.  Once the tables are built, we find the
maximum `L_inc[i]`, backtrack via `P_inc` to reconstruct the actual subsequence,
and do the same for the decreasing case.
"""

def lis_and_lds(pi):
    n = len(pi)
    # L_inc[i]: best length of increasing subsequence ending at i
    # P_inc[i]: previous index in that subsequence
    L_inc = [1] * n
    P_inc = [-1] * n
    # Similarly for decreasing
    L_dec = [1] * n
    P_dec = [-1] * n

    # Build up subproblem solutions in a forward pass
    for i in range(n):
        # Look back at each earlier position j
        for j in range(i):
            # Can we extend an increasing subsequence?
            if pi[j] < pi[i] and L_inc[j] + 1 > L_inc[i]:
                L_inc[i] = L_inc[j] + 1  # update best length
                P_inc[i] = j            # record pointer for backtracking
            # Can we extend a decreasing subsequence?
            if pi[j] > pi[i] and L_dec[j] + 1 > L_dec[i]:
                L_dec[i] = L_dec[j] + 1
                P_dec[i] = j

    # Find the overall best lengths and their end positions
    max_inc_len = max(L_inc)
    end_inc = L_inc.index(max_inc_len)
    max_dec_len = max(L_dec)
    end_dec = L_dec.index(max_dec_len)

    # Backtrack to reconstruct the increasing subsequence
    inc_seq = []
    idx = end_inc
    while idx != -1:
        inc_seq.append(pi[idx])
        idx = P_inc[idx]
    inc_seq.reverse()

    # Backtrack to reconstruct the decreasing subsequence
    dec_seq = []
    idx = end_dec
    while idx != -1:
        dec_seq.append(pi[idx])
        idx = P_dec[idx]
    dec_seq.reverse()

    return inc_seq, dec_seq

# Example usage: read from a simple two-line file
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # First line: n, second line: space-separated permutation
    with open("rosalind_lgis.txt") as f:
        n = int(f.readline().strip())
        pi = list(map(int, f.readline().split()))
    inc, dec = lis_and_lds(pi)
    # Print results: increasing then decreasing
    print(" ".join(map(str, inc)))
    print(" ".join(map(str, dec)))



Dynamic programming: we “look back” at earlier positions and reuse stored best‐lengths (L_inc[j] / L_dec[j]) instead of recomputing.
DP tables (L_inc, L_dec) store the longest subsequence length ending at each index; pointer arrays (P_inc, P_dec) record where to backtrack.
Reconstruction: once the tables are built, find the maximum entry, then follow the pointers backwards to rebuild the subsequence.
Dual use: the same forward‐scan/backtrack pattern yields both increasing and decreasing solutions in one pass (just flip the comparison).

        for symbol in alphabet:

What I Learned

1. Use requests.get(..., stream=True) for binary downloads

You must write binary files using "wb" mode — response.content gives you the raw bytes.
Trying to write response.text on .gz files can cause encoding errors.



2. Compressed .gz files need gzip.open(...) to extract
with gzip.open(gz_filename, "rb") as f_in, open(fa_filename, "wb") as f_out:
    shutil.copyfileobj(f_in, f_out)
-Decompresses file in memory and writes it to a clean .fa file for parsing


3. Create folders dynamically with os.makedirs()
os.makedirs("data", exist_ok=True)
-Prevents crash if folder doesnt exist
-exist_ok=True avoids errors if it does exist already.


4. Use os.path.join() to build safe paths
script_dir = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
data_dir = os.path.join(script_dir, "data")
-Prevents the use of hard coding path directory enabling cross platform usage.

title: Day 25 Rosalind Problem: LCSQ — Longest Common Subsequence
text:
Given two DNA strings in FASTA, return one longest common subsequence (LCS).
Key idea (DP): - Build a table dp[i][j] = LCS length for s[:i] vs t[:j]. - Recurrence: - If s[i-1] == t[j-1]: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 - Else: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) - Backtrack from (m,n) to reconstruct one valid LCS.
Time/space: O(m·n).

title: Day 25 Rosalind Problem: LCSQ — Longest Common Subsequence
text:
Code
"""https://rosalind.info/problems/lcsq/"""
from Bio import SeqIO

"""1Read the two strings from FASTA"""

records = list(SeqIO.parse("rosalind_lcsq.fasta", "fasta"))
s = str(records[0].seq)
t = str(records[1].seq)

m, n = len(s), len(t)

"""2 Building the DP table (m+1) x (n+1)(length of s and t) intially all 0s"""

dp = [[0]*(n+1) for _ in range(m+1)]


for i in range(1, m+1):
    for j in range(1, n+1):
        if s[i-1] == t[j-1]:
            dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1
            """Fill the DP table if previous diagonal left was a match"""
            
        else:
            dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])
            """Fill the DP table if previous diagonal left was not a match"""
            """ this cannot be +1 as it was be reusing the same base 2 times"""

"""3 Backtrack to recover one LCS"""
i, j = m, n
lcs_chars = []

while i > 0 and j > 0:
    if s[i-1] == t[j-1]:
        """when characters match, add to LCS"""
        lcs_chars.append(s[i-1])
        i -= 1
        j -= 1
    elif dp[i-1][j] >= dp[i][j-1]:
        """Deciding route up or down based on DP table values"""
        i -= 1
    else:
        j -= 1

lcs = "".join(reversed(lcs_chars))
print(lcs)

title: Day 25 Rosalind Problem: LCSQ — Longest Common Subsequence
text:
What I Learned
-I recognised it was a DP problem but struggled to remember how to structure the solution.
-Building the `dp` table row by row made me see how each subproblem builds on smaller ones.  
-The rule `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1` for matches is basically saying: *“extend the LCS found so far diagonally.”*  
-For mismatches, taking `max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])` ensures we don’t “lose” progress — we inherit the best subsequence length from either skipping a char in `s` or in `t`.  
-Backtracking was the easiest part:  
    -When characters match, move diagonally and add to the LCS.  
    -Otherwise, move in the direction of the larger value (up or left).  
    -This guarantees we reconstruct a valid subsequence of maximum length.

section: EDIT — Edit Distance (reverse DP, no alignment)
text:
EDIT — Edit Distance (reverse DP, no alignment)
# EDIT — reverse DP to compute Levenshtein edit distance only
# Problem: https://rosalind.info/problems/edit/

from Bio import SeqIO

# Input FASTA file with two records
records = list(SeqIO.parse("rosalind_edit.fasta", "fasta"))
s = str(records[0].seq)
t = str(records[1].seq)

m, n = len(s), len(t)

# DP table: dp[i][j] = min cost to convert s[i:] -> t[j:]

dp = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]

# Initialize outer boundary for reverse DP (base cases)

for j in range(n + 1):
    dp[m][j] = n - j

# Rightmost column: converting s[i:] to empty t[n:] needs (m - i) deletions
for i in range(m + 1):
    dp[i][n] = m - i

# Fill from bottom-right to top-left
for i in range(m - 1, -1, -1):
    for j in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        cost = 0 if s[i] == t[j] else 1
        dp[i][j] = min(
            dp[i + 1][j] + 1,        # delete s[i]
            dp[i][j + 1] + 1,        # insert t[j]
            dp[i + 1][j + 1] + cost  # substitute (or match)
        )

print(dp[0][0])  # minimum edit distance

How it works (EDIT)

State: dp[i][j] stores the minimal cost to transform suffix s[i:] into t[j:].
Transition: Choose the cheapest among delete, insert, substitute/match.
Answer: dp[0][0].

title: Day 27 Rosaand problems — Reverse Dynamic Programming (Reverse DP)
section: EDTA — Edit Distance and Global Alignment (reverse DP + traceback)
text:
EDTA — Edit Distance and Global Alignment (reverse DP + traceback)

Note
This builds on edit distance by adding a traceback loop on top the build DP structure, using 2 unique arrays for each i and j to tally deletions and insertions as -.
# Problem: https://rosalind.info/problems/edta/

from Bio import SeqIO

# Read input (two FASTA records)
records = list(SeqIO.parse("rosalind_edta.fasta", "fasta"))
s = str(records[0].seq)
t = str(records[1].seq)

m, n = len(s), len(t)

# dp[i][j] = min cost to convert s[i:] -> t[j:]
dp = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]

# Initialize boundaries for reverse DP
for j in range(n + 1):
    dp[m][j] = n - j        # empty s to t[j:] needs inserts
for i in range(m + 1):
    dp[i][n] = m - i        # s[i:] to empty t needs deletes

# Fill bottom-right -> top-left
for i in range(m - 1, -1, -1):
    for j in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        cost = 0 if s[i] == t[j] else 1
        dp[i][j] = min(
            dp[i + 1][j] + 1,        # delete s[i]
            dp[i][j + 1] + 1,        # insert t[j]
            dp[i + 1][j + 1] + cost  # substitute (or match)
        )

# Distance
print(dp[0][0])

# Traceback to build one optimal alignment
i, j = 0, 0
aln_s, aln_t = [], []

while i < m or j < n:
    # Prefer diagonal when it matches the optimal cost
    if i < m and j < n and dp[i][j] == dp[i + 1][j + 1] + (0 if s[i] == t[j] else 1):
        aln_s.append(s[i])
        aln_t.append(t[j])
        i += 1
        j += 1
    # Otherwise, delete from s (move down)
    elif i < m and dp[i][j] == dp[i + 1][j] + 1:
        aln_s.append(s[i])
        aln_t.append('-')
        i += 1
    # Otherwise, insert t[j] (move right)
    else:
        aln_s.append('-')
        aln_t.append(t[j])
        j += 1

aln_s = ''.join(aln_s)
aln_t = ''.join(aln_t)

print(aln_s)
print(aln_t)


Traceback rules
At each (i, j) we choose the move consistent with the optimal value stored at dp[i][j]:

Diagonal (match/substitute): if dp[i][j] == dp[i+1][j+1] + (0 or 1).
Delete (from s): if dp[i][j] == dp[i+1][j] + 1 → alignment gets (s[i], '-').
Insert (into s): if dp[i][j] == dp[i][j+1] + 1 → alignment gets ('-', t[j]).

The implemented tie-breaker prefers diagonal, then delete, then insert, which yields one optimal alignment (others may exist with equal cost).

title: Day 27 Rosaand problems — Reverse Dynamic Programming (Reverse DP)
text:
What I Learned
-Reverse DP actually makes a lot of sense once I got used to it — you’re filling the table starting from the “end state” (empty suffixes) and then working back toward the start. It felt weird at first but the traceback becomes pretty natural.
-Initializing the last row/col was a good reminder that these boundaries represent “how many edits it takes if one string is already finished.”
-The traceback rules clicked once I saw how each move (diagonal / delete / insert) is tied directly to which DP transition gave the optimal score.
-There can be multiple optimal alignments, and which one you get depends on how you break ties. My code leans toward diagonal first, which feels intuitive (match/substitute > delete > insert).
-Doing both EDIT (just distance) and EDTA (distance + alignment) side by side really helped me connect how edit distance alone is just the “score,” and EDTA shows you the actual path of edits as an alignment.
-Overall: building the whole thing from scratch gave me way more confidence in DP logic than just memorizing the recurrence formula.

AWS Networking Basics

AWS Direct Connect

Dedicated gigabit connection from an on-premise data center to AWS.

Provides low latency, private connectivity.

Use cases: finance, healthcare, large data transfers.



AWS Virtual Private Network (VPN)

Secure, encrypted connection between on-premise networks and AWS.

Runs over the public internet (unlike Direct Connect).

Cheaper, but higher latency.





Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) & Subnets

Virtual Private Cloud (VPC)

A logically isolated section of the AWS network.

You choose a CIDR IP range for your VPC.

Launch AWS resources (EC2, RDS, etc.) inside.



Subnets

Partition of the VPC IP range into smaller segments.

Each subnet has a smaller CIDR range than the parent VPC.

Route traffic to the appropriate subnet (e.g., public vs private).





Security Groups vs NACLs

Network Access Control Lists (NACLs)

Firewall at the subnet level.

Can create allow and deny rules (e.g., block IP ranges).



Security Groups

Firewall at the instance level.

Allow-only rules (cannot block IPs).

Default deny all, then explicitly allow traffic.

Problem 1: GC Content
Calculate the GC content of multiple DNA strings in FASTA format and identify the one with the highest GC percentage.
My solution
#https://rosalind.info/problems/gc/

from Bio import SeqIO
from Bio.Seq import Seq
from Bio.SeqUtils import gc_fraction
import os


# Get directory of the current script
script_dir = os.path.dirname(os.path.realpath(__file__))
fasta_path = os.path.join(script_dir, "rosalind_gc.fasta")
records = list(SeqIO.parse(fasta_path, "fasta"))

# Track highest GC content and ID
max_gc = 0
max_id = ""
# Loop over each record and calculate GC content
for record in records:
    gc = gc_fraction(record.seq) * 100  # get % value
    if gc > max_gc:
        max_gc = gc
        max_id = record.id

# Print results
print(max_id)
print(f"{max_gc:.6f}")

What I learned:

gc_fraction from Bio.SeqUtils gives clean GC percentages.
Looping through SeqIO records helps to process multiple sequences efficiently.
Comparing and tracking values is easy using standard if logic

Problem 2: Hamming Distance
Compute the number of differing characters between two DNA strings of equal length.
My solution
# https://rosalind.info/problems/hamm/

from Bio import SeqIO
import os


# Get directory of the current script
script_dir = os.path.dirname(os.path.realpath(__file__))
fasta_path = os.path.join(script_dir, "rosalind_hamm.fasta")
records = list(SeqIO.parse(fasta_path, "fasta"))

for i in range(len(records)):
    for j in range(i + 1, len(records)):
        # Calculate Hamming distance
        seq1 = records[i].seq
        seq2 = records[j].seq
        hamming_distance = sum(el1 != el2 for el1, el2 in zip(seq1, seq2))
        print(hamming_distance)

What I learned:

zip(seq1, seq2) lets you pair corresponding elements.
The comparison el1 != el2 returns True for mismatches (which equals 1 when summed).
sum(...) neatly counts total differences without explicit loops.

text:
Problem 2: [Synteny Blocks Have Orientations] (Signed Permutations)(https://rosalind.info/problems/sign/)

Given: A positive integer (n ).
Return: First, the total number of permutations of length (n). Then list every permutation of ({1,2,,n}) (in any order), one per line.

My solution

import itertools  # for generating permutations and all sign combinations
import math

""" Core analogy: signed permutations are like an onion.
# - The outer layer is the ordering (permutation) of the numbers.
# - The inner layers are the signs applied to each position (±) for that ordering.
# Peel one layer at a time: fix an ordering, then explore all sign combinations beneath it.
"""
def main():
    n = 3  # length of the base permutation (1..n)
    numbers = list(range(1, n + 1))  # [1, 2, ..., n]
    output_path = "signed_permutations.txt"  # output file for results

    # Open the file once for writing; the 'with' ensures it closes automatically
    with open(output_path, "w") as f:
        # Compute total number of signed permutations:
        # n! permutations times 2^n choices of sign assignments
        total = math.factorial(n) * (2 ** n)
        f.write(f"{total}\n")  # write the count on the first line

        # Outer loop: iterate over all orderings of [1..n] (the outer onion layer)
        for perm in itertools.permutations(numbers):  # all orderings (n! of them)
            # Inner loop: for each ordering, apply every combination of +/− to each position
            for sign_choice in itertools.product([1, -1], repeat=n):  # 2^n sign vectors
                # Apply sign to each element of the permutation (elementwise multiplication)
                signed_perm = [sign_choice[i] * perm[i] for i in range(n)]
                # Format the signed permutation: include '+' explicitly for positives
                line = " ".join(f"{'+' if x > 0 else ''}{x}" for x in signed_perm)
                f.write(line + "\n")  # write one signed permutation per line

    # Confirmation output to console
    print(f"Wrote {total} signed permutations to {output_path}")

# Immediately invoke main when script runs
main()

What I learned:

Signed permutations structure: n!x2^n = Total permutations = n! independent sign flips = 2^n
Analogy (onion): Fix a permutation (outer layer), then peel through all sign combinations underneath.
Formatting: Explicitly include “+” for positive values to make orientation clear.

title: Role of m6A and METTL3 in Neuroblastoma: TERRA, MYCN, and Therapeutic Implications
text:
Background

TERRA (Telomeric Repeat-containing RNA)

Undergoes altered m⁶A modification.

Localised specifically to telomeres.

Functions in maintaining telomere integrity.

m⁶A methylation and METTL3

METTL3 is essential for telomere maintenance in ALT⁺ cells.

Required for neuroblastoma growth in models where alternative lengthening of telomeres is active.

Also implicated in repressing HOX gene expression, linking epitranscriptomic control to developmental programs.




MYCN and High-Risk Neuroblastoma

MYCN amplification (MNA) is a hallmark of high-risk neuroblastoma.

MYCN expression is regulated by m⁶A-dependent mechanisms.

METTL3 activity supports MYCN-driven oncogenesis.



Therapeutic Angle

Inhibition of METTL3, particularly in combination with MYCN targeting, may offer a promising approach in MNA high-risk neuroblastoma.

This highlights the METTL3–MYCN axis as a potential synthetic vulnerability.



Open Question

Is MYCN expression constant across branching cell lineages, or does it vary depending on its genomic locus?

Understanding this will clarify whether MYCN dependence is uniform across tumour subclones, or context-specific, which has major implications for therapeutic targeting.


Key Takeaways

TERRA is m⁶A-modified and localised at telomeres.

METTL3 is essential in ALT⁺ neuroblastoma for growth and telomere stability.

METTL3 represses HOX genes and supports MYCN expression.

Combining METTL3 inhibition with MYCN-directed therapy could be effective against MNA high-risk neuroblastoma.

title: Variant Filtering in Calcium-Regulating Genes
text:
The goal of this mini-project is to identify genetic variants that might impair calcium-buffering capacity in cancer cells specifically those that could make them more vulnerable to calcium overload triggered by Mastoparan B.
Mastoparan B is known to destabilise the plasma membrane, leading to a spike in intracellular calcium. If certain genes responsible for calcium homeostasis (e.g. PCP4, ATP2B1, BCL2) are disrupted by mutations, it could tip the balance and push the cell toward apoptosis.
This is an early-stage exploration of that hypothesis.

title: Variant Filtering in Calcium-Regulating Genes
text:
Code Snippet
output_path = "mastoparan_variants.txt"
out = open(output_path, "w", encoding="utf-8")

with open(r"C:\Users\zackd\Bioinformatics\clinvar.vcf", "r") as f:
    genes_of_interest = ["PCP4", "BCL2", "ATP2B1", "VDAC1", "RYR1"]

    for line in f:
        if line.startswith("#"):
            continue

        cols = line.strip().split("\t")
        chrom = cols[0].replace("chr", "")
        pos = int(cols[1])
        ref = cols[3]
        alt = cols[4]
        info = cols[7]

        for gene in genes_of_interest:
            if f"GENEINFO={gene}" in info:
                info_dict = dict(item.split("=") for item in info.split(";") if "=" in item)
                significance = info_dict.get("CLNSIG", "NA")
                disease = info_dict.get("CLNDN", "NA")
                review = info_dict.get("CLNREVSTAT", "NA")

                out.write(f"{chrom}:{pos} {ref}>{alt}\n")
                out.write(f"   Significance: {significance}\n")
                out.write(f"   Disease: {disease}\n")
                out.write(f"   Review: {review}\n\n")

out.close()

Interpretation and Context
Right now the code just checks if any known variant touches one of the genes above. It doesn’t check where in the protein the variant lands (e.g. domain, exon, transmembrane), nor does it interpret the functional consequence. But it’s a good starting point.
Variants in calcium-buffering genes might:
Reduce calcium export or sequestration
Increase membrane fragility or ER stress
Accelerate the death response after a calcium spike
This could improve Mastoparan B’s selective cytotoxicity via triggering calcium overload, so any inherent loss-of-buffering could be a weak spot.
